exactFieldDiffsFromProposedV1.before: Jane Addams was born September 6, 1860; she was twenty-seven in April 1888 and twenty-nine on September 18, 1889. In April 1888, Addams attended a bullfight in Madrid and stayed longer than the other travelers, carried by historical associations. She met the others in the foyer; they were pale, disapproving, and affected by the spectacle. She had paid little attention to the bloodshed. That evening she felt deep chagrin and condemned by both the spectacle and the wider moral situation. She judged that her proposed reform had served as an excuse to continue studying and traveling without carrying it out. Her gradually forming plan was to rent a city house among people with unmet needs, where young women could connect study with active life; she could not date its beginning. She resolved to start by talking, then explained the plan to her old school friend Ellen Gates Starr with stumbling, uncertainty, and fear it might collapse when spoken. Starr brought comfort, vigor and enthusiasm; the plan gained substance but remained hazy in detail. In June 1888 Addams visited Toynbee Hall with an introduction, seeking suggestions and firsthand activity. In January 1889 Addams and Starr searched Chicago neighborhoods and described the plan; they intended to begin with their own resources. Thomas Davidson criticized their plan, arguing that communal life could distract residents from the wider neighborhood; their reply did not convince him. She saw an appealing old house from a carriage, searched for it on several days, and eventually gave up. Three weeks later, while searching in the advised neighborhood, she rediscovered the house and felt surprised and overjoyed; some rooms could eventually be sublet. The repaired house had a wide hall and open fireplace; they furnished it with travel photographs, family furniture and durable new pieces suited to its character, taking great pleasure in the work. On September 18, 1889, Addams and Starr moved in with Mary Keyser, who performed housework and became important to household and neighborhood. On the first night they forgot to close or lock a side door and found no theft the next morning, which pleased them. In the first weeks Starr began weekly reading in the upstairs dining room; two members ate with them, helped wash dishes, then cleared the table for photographs. Addams’s early descriptions reported dirty streets, inadequate schools, poor lighting, inadequate sanitation and homes divided among multiple families; many homes had only a backyard water faucet. The first guest was a young woman from a neighboring tenement; her widowed mother helped support their family by scrubbing a downtown theater every night, and the guest stayed a month.

exactFieldDiffsFromProposedV1.before: On November 9, 1847, Blackwell met the anatomy professor at the college. He shook her hand warmly, asked what she had studied, and promised opportunities for the course after she said she had studied all branches but surgery. She handed him an introductory note; he told her to wait in the anteroom while he read it to the assembled class. She heard laughter and concluding applause, entered quietly, and later received help on a missed subject. The letter describes her sitting quietly in the assemblage. Elizabeth Blackwell was born February 3, 1821, and was twenty-six during her 1847 medical-school applications and twenty-seven on graduating January 23, 1849. The November 22 journal describes a dissection as a trying ordeal. Some students blushed or smiled, some held their faces down and shook; she sat grave while her heart palpitated painfully, and afterwards felt nearly worn out. Her sense of propriety was disturbed, though she also found aspects of the exhibition ludicrous. She did not characterize every smile as cruelty and believed some classmates would not want to hurt her feelings. During the November 22 dissection Blackwell called on Christ to help her refrain from smiling, believing that smiling would ruin everything. She sat with grave indifference despite a painfully palpitating heart, regarded the professor's conduct as admirable, and described the day as partly encouraging and in some measure a triumph. These are her attested response and assessments, not proof that prayer caused an outcome; no prayer words or audible delivery are recorded. The November 15 journal records a second operation at which Blackwell was not allowed to be present. The professor's request that she miss some demonstrations annoyed, saddened, and discouraged her; she wrote to him hoping to change this. She believed the exclusion was not his wish, an attested belief rather than a verified motive. It does not identify her physical location while excluded. Blackwell wrote the professor a note asking to be regarded simply as a student with an earnest purpose. She called anatomy serious and worthy of reverence, objected to missing lectures, and offered to yield if the class wanted her absent. November 15 records the writing; November 24 describes its contents. No precise writing location, time, or original full text is supplied. On November 17 the professor appeared pleased with her note and wished to read it to the class the next day; this cheered her. The book records the actual reading in the November 24 entry, not as fulfilled on the earlier proposed date. During the previous day's class, the November 20 journal says a folded paper dropped onto her arms while she took notes. It looked as though it contained writing; she shook it off and continued. A similar action produced a hiss elsewhere, and she felt a light touch on her head. The sender and intent are not independently established. On November 24 the professor read Blackwell's note to the class while she waited in the anteroom. She joyfully heard their hearty approval, entered the amphitheatre, and quietly resumed her place. He said he felt relieved. The following statement of no further difficulty is scoped to this local demonstration dispute. The class reserved her place in lecture rooms, and she could quietly review notes there while waiting for a professor. After enrolling, she decorated her boarding room with reminders of absent friends; anatomy work was arranged with four fellow students, and she studied at night until nearly midnight. In summer hospital study, some resident doctors stopped recording diagnoses and treatment on the cards beside patients' beds, leaving her without that assistance. After graduating she felt she needed substantially more medical experience and continued seeking further study. Blackwell passed her examinations on January 19, 1849. On January 23, after the other graduates received their degrees, she was called alone to the platform and given a medical diploma by the president.

exactFieldDiffsFromProposedV1.before: Charles Darwin was born February 12, 1809; he was twenty-two in August and September 1831. He received the offer late on August 29 and wanted to accept it. The offer was to accompany a captain on a voyage, with natural history collecting, observing and noting; he was not presented as a finished naturalist. His father had not firmly refused but gave advice so strongly against the voyage that Darwin said he could not be comfortable ignoring it. Objections included later steady work, little seafaring, short time for preparation and the chance he might not suit the captain. He said even going with his father’s disapproval would take away energy he needed; without those objections he would have taken the risks. He wrote to refuse, thanked Henslow for the trouble taken, and asked him to send a confirming line in case the badly addressed letter failed to arrive. On the last day of August he visited his uncle’s household, whose members supported going; that evening he drew up his father’s objections. His list included concern the voyage would be useless, uncomfortable, a wild scheme, or another change of profession; his uncle answered the objections. He sent the objection list and uncle’s answers with a new request for a definite yes or no; he promised to yield to a no and stop raising it. He wrote that he would hesitate to go if his father remained uncomfortable and doubted it would unfit him for a steady life. His uncle argued that the voyage had definite work and suited his current interests, while leaving the decision to father and son. On September 1 the uncle sent for Darwin while he was out shooting and offered to take him to see his father; the two traveled together. When they arrived, Darwin’s father kindly gave consent; in his September 2 letter Darwin said his father had changed his mind. After arriving at the Red Lion on September 2, he sent Henslow a note saying he was tired, hoped the place remained open, and wanted to meet next morning. On September 4 he reported spending the preceding day with Henslow considering much that needed to be done; Henslow could supply introductions. Henslow cautioned him against making up his mind until long conversations with the captains; he asked his sister not to spread the news in case he did not go. On September 4, a letter from FitzRoy was so much against Darwin’s going that Darwin and Henslow gave up the scheme; Darwin went to London nevertheless. Darwin met FitzRoy in London on September 5 and found him open, kind and direct; FitzRoy’s intended companion had just written that he could not go. FitzRoy offered to share his cabin and accommodation, though room was scarce; he warned that discomfort in constant company on a small vessel could make both men miserable. FitzRoy said Darwin must live plainly with no wine and the plainest dinners, and advised him not to decide yet; the scheme was less favorable than previously described. FitzRoy directly asked whether Darwin could accept being told to leave the cabin when FitzRoy wanted privacy; Darwin liked that direct approach. The route around the world was not certain, and Darwin said he would not decide until it was settled. On September 6 he reported his first truly cheerful day since the offer, attributing it to his confidence in the captain, while expressly saying the matter was not settled. On September 6 he worked all day adding and removing articles from his lists but would buy nothing until everything was settled. He asked his family for more shirts, slippers, walking shoes, books and instruments needing alteration, and requested an answer by return post. The captain already had many of the books on Darwin’s list, reducing the expected cost of his equipment.

His father advised strongly against it, citing steady employment, preparation and compatibility with the captain. Darwin wrote to decline because ignoring that advice would make him uncomfortable. Early in 1766 he sold goods on a voyage and hoped selling them after returning to Montserrat would provide enough to purchase freedom. The owner ordered the vessel to other ports instead of returning home; Equiano was disappointed and could not invest all his money as profitably at the new stop. On that voyage the vessel also carried enslaved people; his personal trading unfolded within this coercive shipping system. A silversmith became gravely ill; the captain attended him and promised Equiano extra pay after receiving the man’s property. After the death they eagerly opened a nest of trunks. Papers in the smallest were mistaken for valuable notes and the captain clapped his hands. Examination found that the whole nest held only one dollar and a half; all the property could not pay for a coffin. Both men went away mortified. Equiano had nearly enough to purchase freedom even before the anticipated bonus. After returning and selling his goods, he had about 47 pounds and asked the captain how to present the agreed 40-pound sterling purchase price. The captain told him to come one morning when he and the owner were having breakfast together. He entered with money in his hand and fear in his heart, bowed, and asked the owner to keep his promise of freedom when he could pay. The owner recoiled from the request; Equiano heart sank, and the owner questioned whether he had the money and how he earned it. Equiano explained honestly how he obtained the money; the captain confirmed honest earnings and industry. The owner said Equiano had gained money faster than he had and that he would not have made the promise had he expected savings so quickly. At breakfast the captain clapped the owner on the back and urged him to keep the freedom promise and accept payment. He argued that the owner had already profited from Equiano’s work, was now receiving his purchase money back, and could still save money because Equiano would remain with the vessels. The owner said he would keep the promise, accepted the money, and sent Equiano to obtain a written release. His fear turned to joy; he bowed, cried, thanked the men, and left the room to obtain the document. He paid for the document at the register office and took it back to be signed; the owner signed it that day. The reproduced document was signed July 10, 1766 and registered July 11, 1766. It records 70 pounds in island currency; his narrative states 40 pounds sterling. These are distinct currency labels, not contradictory purchase amounts. He remained with the vessel as a paid able-bodied sailor, though he wanted to return to England. During the next voyage in August 1766, an enslaved man insulted and struck him; he lost his temper and beat the man. The other man’s owner threatened to have him publicly flogged. He refused to come ashore and, after repeated advice, hid at a friend’s house. The vessel was searched after he left. Friends demanded return of the warrant before he resumed work; he paid the expenses and returned aboard.

exactFieldDiffsFromProposedV1.before: The state historical marker dates Jacobs birth to about 1813, concealment to 1835 and escape north to 1842; her preface says 27 years in a Slave State. Ages 20–29 deliberately cover this chronological uncertainty. After entering her grandmother’s house, Jacobs was conveyed into the small space beneath the sloping roof. A bed was on the floor, she could not stand upright, and she could sleep on one side but could not turn without hitting the roof. Rats and mice ran over the bed; she was weary and slept. The space admitted neither light nor air; she could turn only by striking the roof. Noises alone marked morning. She suffered for air and found the continued darkness oppressive while sitting or lying cramped without a gleam of light. She heard her children voices below, cried at them, and wanted to speak and see their faces but could find no opening. Relatives passed food up through a concealed door and visited at the opening when it was safe in darkness. While crawling for exercise she struck her head on a small boring tool her carpenter uncle had left behind. She searched for the side facing the street, waited for evening, and bored holes together to make a small opening. She sat at the opening late at night to enjoy a small flow of air; in the morning she watched for her children. She first saw her pursuer, feared the sight, and later saw her children through the opening. Nearly seven years passed in confinement; at times she was listless and at times impatient for air and sunshine, and her cramped body remained painful. The roof deteriorated; her uncle feared repairs would expose her; rain drenched clothes and bedding and worsened bodily pain. A trusted friend arranged passage, but family fear after news of a fugitive killing led her to give up that first plan; she offered the place to another concealed woman. An unexpected visitor entered the storeroom while she was there; she hid behind a barrel and feared discovery, though she later believed the visitor did not see her. Her relatives supported renewed departure; the friend secured a delay of the vessel; she said goodbye and reached it with assistance. The captain led her to a small cabin where the other concealed woman sat; they embraced and she sobbed. The captain heard her sobs, cautioned the women against drawing attention, told them to stay below when another sail was visible, and otherwise allowed deck access. He had represented them as women going to meet husbands. They thanked him and agreed to follow his directions, then talked quietly in the cabin. In the cabin her companion described suffering during escape, fear while concealed at her mother’s house, and separation from all her children at an auction. Jacobs told her about nearly seven years in concealment; the companion scarcely believed it and feared never hearing from her children again. While still near their place of departure she feared being returned, distrusted the crew, and wondered whether the captain could be paid to surrender them. The captain kind manner and her friend report of good treatment reassured her; he invited them onto deck and gave them comfortable seats. Approaching the northern city she watched dawn from the deck with her companion; both had tears and thought themselves safe but had left loved ones behind. After landing a Black minister and his wife offered food and a place to rest, and abolitionist friends offered assistance. When traveling onward she was excluded from first-class cars on racial grounds and endured a crowded unpleasant ride.

Keller tried to seize the doll and grew increasingly angry; Sullivan forced her into a chair and held her until the teacher was nearly exhausted. Sullivan interpreted Keller's anger as believing the doll was being taken away, rather than understanding the spelling exercise. This is the teacher's interpretation, not an independently recorded child statement. After releasing Keller but withholding the doll, Sullivan brought cake, formed its letters, and patted the child's hand. Keller searched unsuccessfully, ran to Sullivan, made her open her mouth very wide, and investigated it. Finding no trace of the cracker, Keller pointed to Sullivan's stomach and spelled eat. By May 16 the teacher and child took long morning walks; Keller asked about things along the way and returned eager to tell her mother. She still made mistakes and tangled words and phrases; Sullivan supplied missing words or sentences.

She arrived in London in autumn 1854; the episode extends to early 1855, so she was 48–49. She had cared for patients in Jamaica and Panama; in London she offered experience and references for army nursing. She questioned whether racial prejudice caused the refusals; this was her suspicion, not established knowledge of the officials’ motives. She describes tears of grief over her motives being doubted, standing still, looking upward at dark clouds and praying aloud. The next morning after a good night’s rest her determination strengthened. She would go on her own responsibility and at her own expense, trusting former patients, doctors and other contacts who already knew her in Jamaica to welcome her. She proposed an independent hotel for invalids and printed cards announcing passage and a mess table and comfortable quarters for sick or recovering officers. She met Thomas Day in England and agreed they might jointly open a store as well as a hotel near the camp. Transferring goods between ships in strong current and wind left her drenched and frightened. On arrival she lodged on an ammunition ship. With no warehouses available their stores were stacked on shore. Her first approach to the sick wharf coincided with the arrival of sick and wounded men. She ran to an artilleryman on a pallet who was groaning, eased his stiff dressings, and heard his groans subside to an uneasy mutter. Small cups of tea stood on the wharf. She raised tea to the man’s dry lips. His hand touched and rested on hers, and he continued holding her hand while she tried to whisper about hope and trust in God. A surgeon approached, shook her hand, thanked her for attending the man and welcomed her help. For six weeks she spent days ashore and nights aboard ship, selling stores under tarpaulin and chiefly assisting transfer of wounded men to hospital transports. The sick-wharf work remained trying. Men who scorned comfort for themselves worried that preparations for the wounded might be late, and others cried while witnessing suffering.

exactFieldDiffsFromProposedV1.before: He asked several places for lodging, but all required money; walking the streets, he passed food stands selling fried chicken and apple pies and could buy nothing. Washington reached Richmond late at night, exhausted, hungry, dirty, out of money, without an acquaintance, and unfamiliar with large cities. He carried a small, cheap satchel containing the few clothes he possessed. Washington left for Hampton in autumn 1872. The NPS chronology gives his birth as April 5, 1856, making him about sixteen; his memoir says his exact birth date was unknown. Exhausted and unable to walk farther, he waited until nobody could see him, then slept beneath an elevated sidewalk with his clothing satchel as a pillow and heard footsteps overhead. At daylight he saw a ship unloading iron and asked its captain to let him work to earn money for food; the captain agreed. He worked long enough to buy breakfast, and the pleased captain offered him continued work for a small daily wage. For several days he unloaded the ship, bought food with small wages, and continued sleeping beneath the sidewalk to save enough money to reach Hampton. After thanking the captain, he reached Hampton with fifty cents and presented himself to the head teacher after a long period without adequate food, washing, or fresh clothes. The head teacher neither admitted nor rejected him initially; he waited near her while she admitted other students, feeling increasingly uncomfortable and wanting a chance. After several hours the teacher asked him to sweep the adjoining classroom; he welcomed the task, having learned careful cleaning in a household job. He swept the room three times and dusted it four times, moved its furniture, cleaned every corner and closet, and reported to the teacher; he felt his future depended on her impression. The teacher inspected the floor and closets and rubbed a handkerchief over woodwork, tables, and benches; finding no dust, she said he could enter the institution. Washington accepted a janitor job that paid nearly all his board; its hard work included caring for many rooms, working late, rising early to build fires, and preparing lessons. The head teacher provided advice and encouragement during difficulties. He borrowed books, lacked clothing, washed his single pair of socks at night, and received used clothing from teachers. His janitor work eventually paid all his board, but tuition remained unaffordable; Armstrong found Morgan to pay his tuition.
